title: The Desert Blooms and the Redeemed Return
summary: The wilderness will rejoice and blossom, receiving the glory of Lebanon, Carmel, and Sharon, and the people will see the glory of the LORD. The fearful are told to be strong, because God is coming to save, and when he comes the blind will see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, and water will burst out in the desert. A highway called the Way of Holiness will carry the redeemed safely home to Zion with everlasting joy, while sorrow and sighing flee.
story: Chapter 35 is the bright partner of chapter 34. There a land became a wilderness of thorns and wild creatures; here the wilderness becomes a garden and a road. Together the two chapters close the poetry of the book's first half. Chapter 35 also reaches forward: its highway, its call to strengthen the weak, and its promise that God is coming anticipate almost word for word the opening of chapter 40, "Comfort, comfort My people." Between them stand the narratives of chapters 36 to 39, which show Jerusalem's deliverance from Assyria and then point ahead to Babylon. Chapter 35 is the horizon beyond both crises.
historical:
The chapter's setting is tied to the debate over chapters 34 and 35. On the traditional view Isaiah wrote it in the eighth century BC, looking beyond the Assyrian crisis to a far greater restoration. Many critical scholars date it to the exile or after, since it seems to assume a people scattered far from Zion and it shares much of its language with chapters 40 to 55, which address the exiles in Babylon in the sixth century BC. Some have suggested that it was composed to link the two halves of the book. Whatever its date, it would have been heard by exiles who faced a long road home across real desert: the route from Babylon to Judah ran for hundreds of miles, usually following the Euphrates northwest before turning south, and the return that began after Cyrus's decree of 539 or 538 BC was hard and slow.

The places named in verse 2, Lebanon, Carmel, and Sharon, were the most fertile and beautiful regions of the land. In 33:9 they withered in mourning; here their glory is given to the desert. The reversal answers the devastation of the Assyrian invasion and, for later readers, the ruin of Judah by Babylon.
cultural:
For people in the ancient Near East, the desert was the place of danger and death: no water, no shade, lions and wild beasts, and bandits along the roads. Blooming crocus or rose (the Hebrew flower is uncertain, perhaps a crocus or asphodel) and bursting streams describe the most dramatic change imaginable. Papyrus and reeds (verse 7) grew only in marshes and along rivers, so their appearance where jackals once lived means the land has become well watered.

Kings in the ancient world built processional roads for their gods and for their own victory parades. Babylon's Processional Way, leading through the Ishtar Gate, is a famous example. Isaiah's highway is a road of pilgrimage and return, reserved for the holy and the redeemed, and so safe that no lion can go on it. The two words for redemption in verses 9 and 10 come from family law. A redeemer (goel) was a relative responsible to buy back family land or a family member sold into slavery, as Boaz does in Ruth 4, and ransom (padah) described the price paid to free someone. God takes that role for his people.
literary: The chapter is a single, carefully shaped poem. Verses 1 and 2 open with the joy of the land itself, then verses 3 and 4 turn to people, with a direct command to strengthen the weak and a quoted message for the fearful. Verses 5 to 7 are built on the word "Then," listing healings of the body (blind, deaf, lame, mute) alongside the healing of the land (waters in the wilderness, springs in parched ground), so that human and natural renewal are woven together. Verses 8 to 10 describe the highway and those who walk on it. The poem ends with a strong closing couplet: gladness and joy overtake the redeemed, and sorrow and sighing flee. Verse 10 appears again, almost word for word, in 51:11, one of the clearest links between the two halves of the book.

outline.t: The wilderness rejoices and sees the glory of the LORD
Strengthen the weak: your God will come to save
Healing for the body and water in the desert
The Way of Holiness and the joyful return to Zion

doctrines.note: Salvation here is God's coming to rescue his people (verse 4), and it reaches body, land, and community. The blind, deaf, lame, and mute are healed, and the redeemed return home with joy.
The chapter is a picture of the end God intends: a renewed creation, a people restored, and sorrow gone. It gives the weak and fearful a reason to stand firm now.
The road home is the Way of Holiness. Redemption does not lead to a life indifferent to God's character; the redeemed walk on a road set apart for him.

words.note: Gaal, to redeem. The verb comes from family law, where a near relative bought back land or freed a family member from slavery. When the LORD is called redeemer, especially in chapters 40 to 66, the word presents him as the relative who takes responsibility for his people at his own cost. In verse 9 the redeemed are those he has claimed.

Padah, to ransom. It describes releasing someone by paying a price, as with the redemption of the firstborn (Exodus 13:13). In verse 10 the ransomed of the LORD return to Zion; the word underlines that their freedom was secured by someone else.

Maslul, highway. This word appears only here in the Old Testament and describes a raised, built-up road. Its close relative mesillah is used in 40:3 for the highway prepared in the desert for God. Here the highway is for the redeemed, called the Way of Holiness.

christ: When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus answered by pointing to what was happening: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear (Matthew 11:4-5; Luke 7:22), language drawn from this chapter and from Isaiah 61. He was presenting his healings as the signs that God had come to save, as verse 4 promised. The Letter to the Hebrews applies verse 3 to Christians under discipline, urging them to strengthen their weak hands and feeble knees (Hebrews 12:12). The Gospels also connect the highway in the desert with the ministry of John the Baptist, though they quote Isaiah 40:3 rather than this chapter. The full picture, a renewed creation and sorrow gone forever, is the hope the New Testament places in Christ's return (Revelation 21:4).
questions: Verse 3 commands the strong to strengthen the limp hands and feeble knees of others. Who around you needs that kind of help?
The chapter weaves together the healing of people and the renewal of the land. What does that suggest about the scope of God's salvation?
The redeemed walk a road called the Way of Holiness. How does being rescued by God change the way a person lives?
